newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: Falklands reject extended Argentine cemetery visits.
newsitem.headline: Falklands reject extended Argentine cemetery visits.

text.p: Falkland councillors have refused to allow extended visits by Argentine relatives grieving for soldiers killed in the 1982 conflict with Britain over the remote islands.
Instead, the councillors want the relatives to fly in together via Chile for a one-off visit under the auspices of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

Britain, which went to war with Argentina over the south Atlantic islands in a conflict that cost 1,000 lives, had asked that Argentine relatives be allowed to visit the Falklands in a series of visits over several weeks.

But Councillor Eric Goss said they favoured a one-day visit by relatives to the cemetery. It is tucked away on a desolate headland that can only be reached by a four-wheel drive vehicle capable of tackling the soggy terrain.
Falklands Governor Richard Ralph said he favoured visits by small groups of Argentine relatives spread over several weeks. Each group would stay overnight in a lodge at the remote Darwin settlement.
"We do not like that proposal," Goss said.

"We are not happy at the prospect of groups of Argentines wandering around Darwin and Goose Green as they would be hard to control. So we favour a one-off visit by a large group using a large aircraft under the auspices of the ICRC."
The first organised visit by Argentine next-of-kin took place in March 1991 when 354 relatives visited the remote, windswept cemetery where 234 Argentine servicemen are buried.
Many wept uncontrollably and threw themselves on the graves. Priests and doctors tried to comfort them.
The pro-British islanders are still deeply mistrustful of a country that continues to lay claim to the islands it calls the Malvinas. The scars of war, even in victory, are slow to heal.
Only 111 of the bodies were ever identified. Many of the crosses in the forlorn lines are marked with the one word "Conscripto" or "Soldado" (soldier).
Others bear the simple inscription in English: "An Argentine soldier known unto God."

In 1994, the bodies of five Argentine Air Force members were discovered on Pebble Island and buried with full military honours. Their relatives were allowed in the next year for a service of consecration.
